papers.title: A cytoskeletal toggle switch controls amnion architecture and fate
papers.abstract: Binary cellular decisions are generally attributed to gene regulatory networks, with cytoskeletal-driven shape changes often treated as an output. Yet, whether the cytoskeleton can itself implement switch-like logic to drive abrupt morphological transitions remains unknown. In the primate amniotic sac, the extraembryonic amnion derives directly from the columnar epiblast and abruptly flattens into a squamous epithelium to form a highly asymmetric cavity. Here, we identify a cytoskeletal switch driving this developmental bifurcation in human gastrula models. Mutual inhibition between actomyosin and keratin networks generates two mechanical attractors: amnion cells flip into a keratin-rich, squamous shape, while the epiblast remains myosin-rich and columnar. Ectopic activation of YAP1-TEAD signaling triggers the myosin-keratin switch without inducing amnion specification, establishing that the switch is not simply a consequence of fate changes. Conversely, preventing the switch disrupts amnion specification, showing that this shape bifurcation gates lineage commitment. Single-cell transcriptomics across cytoskeletal perturbations revealed a transcriptional signature for the toggle switch, which is recapitulated in vivo in the human and marmoset amnion. Together, our findings show that the cytoskeleton acts not only as an effector of tissue shape but as a decision-making module, implementing the same toggle switch logic as gene regulatory networks to drive morphological bifurcations.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Orthologous ANK-NLR-WRKY Proteins in Wheat Species: Evolutionary Divergence and Structural Characteristics
papers.abstract: The plant nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors are known to play a crucial role in plant host defence against a variety of biotic stresses. Several NLR proteins contain integrated domains (NLR-ID) like ankyrin (ANK) and WRKY transcription factor domains and are important evolutionary adaptations in plant immunity. They are responsible for the perception of effector molecules from invading pathogens and pests and subsequent activation of plant immune responses. However, the functional roles these ANK-NLR-WRKY proteins play in wheat (Triticum aestivum) against various pathogens and pests remain poorly understood. Computational tools employed for comparative sequence and phylogenetic analyses revealed that TaAdnr1 is highly conserved across diploid (T. urartu), tetraploid (T. dicoccoides), and hexaploid (T. aestivum) wheat species, including its well characterised orthologue YrU1 from T. urartu. Three-dimensional (3D) protein structural modelling using AlphaFold2 supported strong conservation in the multiple domains of these NLR orthologues, more specifically within the integrated WRKY domain. This conservation may suggest a strong evolutionary maintenance of TaADNR1. Furthermore, this may also suggest TaADNR1 reflects specificity in effector recognition and regulation. Therefore, the integration of functional genomics studies, sequence analysis, evolutionary analysis and structural modelling possesses the potential to provide new insights into the pleiotropic roles of integrated domain NLRs in wheat.

papers.title: How gradual evolution, fitness landscapes, and trait associations shape mutation rates in large populations
papers.abstract: Mutation rates are evolvable traits that respond to selection partly through the associations of modifier alleles with other variants affecting individual fitness. Yet, these variants can be subject to various selective regimes, whose respective role in shaping the evolution of mutation rates remains incompletely understood. To clarify the links between the fitness landscape and selection on mutation rates, we analyse a multi-locus continuum-of-alleles model where traits can affect both individual fitness and the mutation rates expressed across loci. We obtain a closed hierarchical system of moments describing the change in the distribution of traits, and thus in mutation rates, under small trait variation. We find that variation in mutation rates across individuals builds skew in the trait distribution, which plays a key role in the evolution of mutation rates; to track such asymmetries, we go beyond classical normal closure and adapt a cumulant-neglect method. We show that positive mutation rates are favoured by indirect selection out of evolutionary equilibrium (under directional, fluctuating or diversifying selection) and selected against at equilibrium (under homogenising selection). We illustrate these cases with a two-trait model, which we also study using individual-based simulations to evaluate the robustness of our deterministic results to genetic drift. Beyond these examples, our results classify the selective mechanisms acting on mutation rates and rank their importance according to the local shape of the fitness landscape and the variational properties of the population. This provides an account of the different ways selection can act on transmission fidelity in large populations.

papers.title: The virome of New Zealand fur seals reveals novel viral diversity and evidence of continued Canine distemper virus circulation
papers.abstract: Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaik[o]ura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaik[o]ura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaik[o]ura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.

papers.title: Body-wide microbial ecosystem reorganization across the cognitive impairment spectrum in Parkinsons disease
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a major determinant of disability in Parkinsons disease (PD), yet how microbial alterations across multiple body sites accompany cognitive dysfunction remains poorly understood. We characterized microbial communities from five body sites (stool, saliva, tongue, nasal cavity, and axilla) in 150 participants spanning healthy controls, PD with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and PD dementia (PDD), generating 616 samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis v2 (MOFA2) identified a multisite microbial signature with prominent oral and gut contributions that varied across clinical groups (Factor 8; {beta} = -0.58, p < 0.0001). MintTea analysis identified stable multisite microbial assemblies associated with cognitive status, including a module distinguishing PD-MCI from PDD (in-sample AUROC = 0.810). Core microbiome analysis revealed a net reduction of 45 genus-site core memberships across four anatomical sites in cognitively impaired participants, including reduced prevalence of the butyrate-associated genus Roseburia. Multivariable models incorporating microbial signatures and demographic covariates explained an average of 35.4% of cognitive-outcome variance, with microbial features contributing an additional 8.0 percentage points beyond age, sex, and education. Procrustes analysis revealed a pronounced, non-linear pattern of weakening cross-site microbial community correspondence at the dementia stage. The Global Body-wide Organization Index remained relatively stable between HC (0.335) and PD-MCI (0.341) but declined to 0.257 in PDD, representing a 23% reduction relative to HC. Together, these findings identify disease-associated multisite microbial signatures and altered core-community composition across the PD cognitive impairment spectrum, supporting further investigation of multisite microbiome profiling for cognitive stratification.

papers.title: Integrating Biometric, Metabolic, and Photochemical Traits to Identify Candidate Physiological Indicators of Salinity Tolerance and Forage Quality in Alfalfa Cultivars
papers.abstract: Salinity limits alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) productivity, yet integrative physiological markers of cultivar tolerance remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify candidate physiological indicators of salt tolerance by integrating growth, metabolic, and time-resolved photosynthetic traits across diverse alfalfa cultivars. We exposed nine alfalfa cultivars to a 200 mM NaCl hydroponic shock and monitored their physiological responses over 14 days. We assessed shoot and root growth, leaf Na+/K+ homeostasis, carbohydrate partitioning, dynamic chlorophyll a fluorescence (ChlF), and NIRS-based forage quality. Salinity elicited cultivar-dependent responses. Tolerant cultivars maintained shoot biomass, restricted foliar Na+ accumulation, preserved leaf starch reserves, and progressively recovered Phi2 and linear electron flow (LEF) following initial declines. In contrast, less tolerant cultivars showed persistent growth inhibition, reduced leaf starch, and persistent photochemical impairment. At 7 and 14 dpt, PItotal and Fv'/Fm' correlated positively with final biomass, whereas PhiNPQ and PhiNO showed negative correlations. Notably, the association between regulated energy dissipation (PhiNPQ) and biomass retention inverted over time, shifting from an early photoprotective mechanism at 1 dpt to a sign of chronic photoinhibitory strain by 7 and 14 dpt. These responses were accompanied by cultivar-specific changes in Na+/K+; balance, soluble sugars, starch, and forage quality. Tracking time-resolved PSII photochemistry reveals that maintaining PItotal and Fv'/Fm' under saline stress offers an accurate, non-invasive proxy for evaluating cultivar resilience. Their integration into high-throughput phenotyping and breeding programs could facilitate the selection of resilient cultivars. Field validation should consider both biomass production and forage nutritional quality.

papers.title: A trade-off shaping leaf mesophyll architecture emerges from a stochastic geometry model
papers.abstract: Leaf mesophyll architecture has a great impact on plant functions, including photosynthesis. Yet, understanding the principles governing growth, stability, and interspecific variation of leaf mesophyll architecture remains elusive. Here, we develop a computational framework based on stochastic space tessellation to simulate two-dimensional paradermal slices of leaf spongy mesophyll across 40 vascular plant species using three data-derived parameters: leaf porosity, cell arm length, and cell arm diameter. The framework successfully reconstructs leaf slices while preserving six biological, topological, and cell-level traits, with one- to three-armed cell geometries generally outperforming circular cells. Importantly, we further develop a theoretical model based on stochastic geometry that closely agrees with the simulations and reveals that leaf porosity strongly influences cell wall construction cost, while cell-arm statistics shape this relationship. Our parsimoniously parameterized model provides a basis for optimizing leaf architecture to maximize carbon dioxide uptake while minimizing cell wall construction costs.

papers.title: ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 coordinates lipid homeostasis to support autophagosome formation
papers.abstract: Autophagosome formation requires cells to mobilize lipids for phagophore expansion and completion while maintaining lipid homeostasis during nutrient stress. How lipid intermediates are partitioned between membrane synthesis and neutral lipid storage under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 as a regulator of starvation-induced autophagy in budding yeast. Loss of Mdm1 reduced autophagic flux despite preserved TORC1 responses to starvation and impaired autophagosome completion, as indicated by the accumulation of perivacuolar Atg8-positive structures and reduced protease protection. Lipidomic analyses revealed decreased phosphatidylinositol (PI) in whole cells and Atg8-enriched membrane fractions, accompanied by increased diacylglycerol (DAG) and storage lipids. Derepression of phospholipid synthesis through OPI1 deletion or inhibition of triacylglycerol synthesis restored autophagic flux. Remarkably, exogenous DAG also rescued autophagy despite elevated endogenous DAG in Mdm1-deficient cells. DAG supplementation increased PI abundance and improved protease protection, linking changes in lipid metabolism to autophagosome completion. Together, these findings implicate Mdm1 in coordinating membrane phospholipid homeostasis with neutral lipid metabolism and suggest that the metabolic availability of lipid intermediates contributes to efficient autophagosome formation during starvation.

papers.title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
papers.abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

papers.title: Depth-partitioned oxidation of atmospheric hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane in a glacier forefield soil
papers.abstract: Glacier forefields are model systems for pioneer ecosystem assembly under extreme oligotrophy. Their microbial communities carry widespread genomic potential to oxidize atmospheric trace gases, yet whether this potential is transcribed in situ, and by which lineages, remains largely untested. Here we combined depth-resolved profiling of hydrogen (H2), carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH4) at ten locations in the Wildstrubel glacier forefield, Swiss Alps, with mesocosm experiments, long-read metagenomics, and genome-resolved metatranscriptomics. Soils were consistent net sinks for atmospheric H2 and CH4, with fluxes ~2-fold and ~6-fold higher, respectively, in older than in younger terrain. H2 uptake was concentrated in the upper 20 cm, whereas CH4 uptake extended deeper. In the field, CO uptake was masked by apparent subsurface production, but in mesocosms lacking this source both CO and H2 were drawn below atmospheric concentrations. Although 57% of metagenome-assembled genomes encoded trace-gas oxidation enzymes, topsoil transcription was dominated by Group 1h [NiFe]-hydrogenases from a few Actinomycetota populations, in which the CO dehydrogenase coxL was transcribed 20- to 35-fold less. The second most transcribed marker was smoX, most closely related to C2-C6 alkane monooxygenases, suggesting the use of short-chain alkanes of possible subsurface origin. Mobile genetic elements were widely transcribed, matching host transcription, but a 104-kb plasmid-borne coxMSL operon was largely silent. Acetylene perturbation induced no detectable switching between trace-gas pathways. Together, these data suggest that trace-gas metabolism is partitioned across soil depth: atmospheric H2 scavenging dominates topsoil transcription, whereas methanotrophy and CO production occur deeper. Net surface fluxes, particularly for CO, therefore, underestimate gross trace-gas turnover.

papers.title: Flow Virometry-Based Profiling of Viral Population Diversity
papers.abstract: Viruses exhibit great phenotypic heterogeneity. Flow virometry enables high-throughput analysis of phenotypic diversity in viral populations, while flow-based sorting allows subpopulations to be isolated for separate characterization. Despite their advantages, flow virometry and sorting have not yet been widely adopted in virology partly because of limited protocols and underexplored applications. Here, we provide a practical guide for analyzing and quantifying virus particles from diverse families using flow virometry enhanced by fluorescence labeling. We further explore applications beyond basic and static characterization of virus populations. We demonstrate that flow virometry can report on interactions between virions and binding partners, as well as between virions. It provides a particle denominator that, combined with genome copy measurements, enables estimation of viral population ploidy. We also show how dynamic processes, such as viral membrane fusion, can be measured in real time. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of sorting virions based on their intrinsic properties, such as morphology, for downstream study. This practical guide provides a roadmap for wider implementation of flow virometry in virology, while the applications illustrated here demonstrate potential to address a variety of questions about virion properties, interactions, and dynamics at the single-particle level.

papers.title: Surrogate Verifiers Shape Decisions in Closed-Loop Experimental Design
papers.abstract: High throughput, automated screening has revolutionized biological experimentation and prompted predictions of AI-enabled "self-driving" labs. Deployed autonomous lab systems typically use a learned surrogate to predict new experimental candidates and rank which conditions deserve expensive follow-up. Determining whether a computational surrogate verifier can substitute for an experimental assay's ground truth requires an understanding of model accuracy, uncertainty, and extrapolation. In this work, we present surrogate verifiers trained on N=7,688 Lacticaseibacillus growth curves exploring a 10-dimensional media component experimental design space. We train surrogate models across six distinct families including polynomial, Gaussian-process, tree-ensemble, neural, and Monod-kinetic forms to predict maximum optical density (OD600). Surrogates ranked by the most commonly reported accuracy metrics (held-out R^2; MAE; RMSE) disagree sharply on which experiments to test next and the best achievable yield. We evaluate models in a Bayesian optimization loop and find that the model used as the active learning oracle matters more than the acquisition function or batch size. We apply conformal calibration to build a model-agnostic assessment criterion of uncertainty and model coverage. We end by evaluating model accuracy and calibration under transfer to an unseen related bacterial strain, and confirm on a prospective validation plate that the transferred verifier's intervals fail in the direction and region our retrospective analysis predicts. This work explores the surrogate verifier within the loop as a previously underexplored axis of closed-loop design and points towards best calibration practices.

papers.title: Connexin43 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and organelle stress in BRAF-mutant melanoma cells
papers.abstract: Metabolic flexibility helps cancer cells survive targeted therapy, and BRAF-mutant melanoma rewires mitochondrial metabolism in response to BRAF/MEK inhibitors (BRAF/MEKi). We previously showed that connexin43 (Cx43) acts as a tumour suppressor in BRAF-mutant melanoma and enhances the response to BRAF/MEKi. Here, we investigated whether mitochondrial remodelling contributes to these effects. Cx43 upregulation promoted mitochondrial biogenesis including selective increase of CI and CV, enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, alongside DRP1-associated mitochondrial fragmentation. Despite enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS, Cx43 upregulation was associated with respiratory chain remodelling, characterised by loss of complex IV, increased ER and mitochondrial stress, and enhanced mTORC1-associated signalling. These changes were accompanied by an adaptive unfolded protein response that did not engage the pro-apoptotic ATF4-CHOP axis. Notably, BRAF/MEK inhibition largely attenuated the mitochondrial biogenesis phenotype and most of the stress markers associated with Cx43 upregulation, while promoting mitochondrial network elongation and markedly increasing mitochondrial ROS. Despite this impact, Cx43-expressing tumour cells retained higher membrane potential, ROS levels and survival under glucose-limiting conditions. Collectively, these findings reveal a dissociation between the mitochondrial effects of Cx43 and its enhancement of the response to BRAF/MEKi, highlighting the complexity of Cx43-mediated metabolic regulation in BRAF-mutant melanoma. By distinguishing mitochondrial remodelling from therapeutic sensitisation, this study provides new insights into the response to BRAF/MEK inhibition and highlights mTORC1-associated signalling and mitochondrial oxidative stress as potential therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.

papers.title: Radiation survival selects clonally restricted NSCLC survivors with impaired metastatic capacity and distinct bioenergetic states
papers.abstract: Radiation resistance and recurrence remain major challenges in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Whether radiation survival enriches for more aggressive, metastasis-competent cells remains unresolved. Using longitudinal cellular barcoding, functional assays, and multi-omics profiling in diverse NSCLC models, we show that fractionated irradiation imposes a strong clonal bottleneck, but recovery follows either stochastic or deterministic trajectories. Despite this diversity, all radiation-surviving populations exhibit increased radiosensitivity and profoundly impaired metastatic capacity, including near-complete failure in lung colonization in vivo. Transcriptomic and metabolic analyses reveal three distinct bioenergetic states, hypermetabolic, energy-conserving, and metabolically suppressed, each supported by unique transcriptional programs. Crucially, clonal dominance does not predict molecular or functional state, indicating that clonal selection and post-irradiation reprogramming are decoupled. These findings challenge the assumption that radiation selects for aggressive clones and reveal that radiation survival may instead create a state of post-irradiation vulnerability. This has important implications for therapy: targeting adaptive pathways, not just resistant clones, may improve outcomes.

papers.title: Within- and transgenerational plasticity evolve separately in a thermally adapted ectotherm
papers.abstract: Climate change is imposing strong selection pressures on many wild populations, forcing them to adapt or face extinction. Conservation biology attempts to predict evolutionary responses to inform management but is hampered by a poor understanding of how variation arises. For many populations, responses to warming may rely substantially upon phenotypic plasticity, with cues from parental and offspring environments shaping development. However, how information from the environment, the genome, and the epigenome interacts to produce phenotypic variation is poorly understood. We investigated these factors, and their interactions, by using Icelandic populations of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) that have adapted to geothermal warming. Using a split-temperature F1 to F2 hybrid cross, a novel morphometric approach, and reduced representation bisulphite sequencing, we elucidated the genetic architecture of transgenerational plasticity (TGP), within-generation plasticity (WGP), and that of morphological and methylation variation. This revealed that TGP and WGP have distinct genetic architectures involving different biological functions. The genetic architecture of traits was strongly influenced by both the parental and offspring thermal environments, potentially exposing different genetic variation to selection. Finally, we showed that TGP is favoured by selection and driven by the exposure of allelic variation by methylation. Our results suggested that predicting climate change responses should move beyond assessments of standing genetic variation to understand how TGP, WGP and the environment interact. More broadly, these findings improve our understanding of the processes that generate variation during adaptive divergence.

papers.title: Shaped by shape: costs and topology drive host-parasite evolution in spatial networks
papers.abstract: How disease spreads across space is well studied, but how the topology of spatial networks shapes host-parasite evolution is less understood. Host-parasite interactions unfold across spatial networks in which populations differ in the number of neighbours, yet most theory has focused on regular networks such as grids. Here, we embed a multilocus gene-for-gene infection model into a metapopulation to investigate host-parasite coevolution across empirically inspired and synthetic spatial networks. We find that variation in the number of neighbours generates spatial variation in local host density and parasite prevalence, creating a network-wide mosaic of ecological conditions for selection. Greater variation in the number of neighbours, or higher degree heterogeneity, promotes the evolution of host resistance. The same degree heterogeneity leads to reduced parasite infectivity in well-connected patches versus higher infectivity in patches with fewer neighbours. Both outcomes arise because populations with fewer neighbours experience net host outflux and reduced prevalence, whereas populations with more neighbours accumulate hosts and experience different selective pressures. Dispersal both drives and homogenises host resistance across the network, while maintaining spatial structure in parasite infectivity. We here identify a topology-epidemiology-evolution feedback impacting coevolution even when populations experience identical environmental conditions. Across network types, coevolutionary outcomes are driven by the network's degree heterogeneity, which can be quantified using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index in real landscapes. Our results provide testable predictions for how changes in network topology can shape the evolution of host resistance and parasite infectivity.

papers.title: SBP transcription factors repress maize brace root initiation and regulate primordia expansion
papers.abstract: Nodal roots are critical determinants of maize productivity and resilience, but the molecular mechanisms governing their development remain poorly defined. Transcriptome analyses across three stages of maize brace root (aboveground nodal roots) development identified the squamosa promoter binding protein (SBP) transcription factors tasselsheath4 (TSH4), unbranched2 (UB2), and unbranched3 (UB3) as negative regulators of brace root initiation. Analysis of single, double, and triple mutants revealed a dose-dependent increase in the number of nodes with brace roots and a non-linear increase in the number of brace roots per node. The increased number of brace roots within a node resulted from a physical expansion of the stem pulvinus and de-repression of brace root initiation programs, which resulted in two tiers of brace roots at each node. Downstream analyses revealed that SBP TFs negatively regulate liguleless2 expression, which acts in concert with liguleless1 to promote brace root initiation, and phytohormone analysis identified a mechanism whereby sbp mutants exhibited increased ACC accumulation. Differential levels of gibberellin (GA4) were identified between tsh4 and ub2;ub3 mutant nodes. The differential levels of gibberellin regulated primordia expansion resulting in distinct brace root phenotypes - tsh4 mutants had fewer, thicker brace roots whereas ub3 mutants had more and thinner brace roots. The tsh4 and ub3 GA4-mediated post-initiation expansion mechanism was also found to underlie natural variation in brace root size and number. Together, our findings identify SBP transcription factors as central regulators of brace root initiation and primordia expansion and show that altering developmental trajectories can alter brace root architecture.

papers.title: Mitochondria morphology changes dynamically during germ cell differentiation and under chemical stress in C. elegans: a quantitative ultrastructural study.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dynamics are essential for cellular health and fertility, yet how mitochondrial ultrastructure adapts during gametogenesis and acute environmental stress remains poorly understood. Here, using high-pressure freezing electron microscopy and automated quantitative morphometry (EMito-Metrix), we mapped mitochondrial ultrastructure across the Caenorhabditis elegans germline and somatic tissues. We reveal that mitochondria undergo progressive structural maturation during germ cell differentiation, transitioning from small, round profiles to elongated networks with aligned cristae. Following short oxidative stress, differentiating germ cells and early embryos, unlike somatic or sperm cells, undergo a remarkable morphological remodeling to form protective, fusion-dependent donut-shaped and vacuolated spheroid mitochondria. Genetic disruption of the mitochondrial fusion factor fzo-1 blocks this pathway and results in a collapse of stress-induced brood size. These results demonstrate that atypical mitochondrial morphotypes are not passive markers of damage, but an active, FZO-1-dependent defense strategy shielding female gametes. This work highlights the C. elegans gonad as a versatile model to explore mitochondrial plasticity, reproductive aging, and environmental toxicology.

papers.title: A dynamic role for the apical extracellular matrix in cell migration during Drosophila abdominal morphogenesis
papers.abstract: Cell migration plays a central role in development, ensuring cells reach their correct destinations. Many migratory cell types require interaction with the extracellular matrix (ECM) to generate traction. While the basal ECM (bECM) is well known for its role in cell motility, the apical ECM (aECM) has mostly been shown to provide structural and mechanical support during morphogenesis and remains less understood. In Drosophila, the aECM is primarily composed of the giant protein Dumpy (Dpy), which interacts with the Zona Pellucida (ZP) domain protein Piopio (Pio). In this study, we elucidate the role of the aECM in the formation of the adult abdominal epidermis of Drosophila. During this process, the larval epithelial cells (LECs) transition from a stationary to a mobile state, in which they migrate directionally, before apically constricting and undergoing apoptosis. Using in vivo 4D microscopy, we examined the role of the aECM in the dynamic behaviour of the LECs. Initially, a layer of Dpy and Pio is located apically to the stationary LECs. As migration begins, the LECs leave behind this early layer while depositing an additional, morphologically distinct layer of Dpy. Knock-down of Dpy or Pio leads to the detachment of stationary LECs from the early layer and, subsequently, to impaired LEC migration. Our results reveal that the aECM transitions from acting as an anchoring scaffold to supporting cell migration. This functional change is closely linked to the change in LEC behaviour. Together, these findings identify the aECM as a substrate for cell migration and highlight a dynamic role of the aECM during morphogenesis.

papers.title: Spatial coordination of peptidoglycan synthesis by MreB directs morphogenesis in Xanthomonas citri
papers.abstract: The cytoskeletal proteins MreB and FtsZ coordinate cell wall synthesis during elongation and division in rod shaped bacteria. How these two systems interact in the citrus canker pathogen Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri (X. citri) remains unclear. Previously, we showed that disruption of FtsZ ring placement, by deletion of minC, uncouples cell wall synthesis from division, leading to branching and filamentation. Now, using a MreB-GFP sandwich fusion, we show that MreB localizes at the inner membrane, independently of MinC. Peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis (visualized with the fluorescent D-amino acid analogue HADA) happens mostly at the division septum. Perturbation of MreB with A22 disrupts rod shape maintenance and leads to a dose-dependent growth inhibition. A22 induces a reversible relocalization of MreB into the cell cap region, which is accompanied by a shift of PG synthesis from midcell to the poles. This indicates that MreB is required for proper spatial regulation of PG insertion. This loss of spatial control is exacerbated in {Delta}minC cells, which display increased A22 sensitivity, indicating a synthetic dependence on MreB when FtsZ ring placement is affected. Furthermore, MreB inhibition disrupts ParABS-mediated chromosome segregation, leading to anucleate cells. Our findings establish MreB as a key coordinator of cell wall synthesis, cell shape, and chromosome segregation in X. citri

papers.title: Comparative exometabolome and extracellular-vesicle metabolome of Bifidobacterium
papers.abstract: Bifidobacterium species are early colonisers of the human gut and are widely used as probiotics, yet their extracellular chemistry remains largely unexplored, and the small-molecule cargo of their extracellular vesicles (EVs) has not been characterised. We carried out an exploratory, descriptive characterisation of the exometabolome and EV metabolome of Bifidobacterium longum 35624 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis at 24 and 48 h of anaerobic growth, using untargeted LC MS/MS coupled with feature-based molecular networking and semi-targeted analysis of conjugated lipids. The two strains reshaped the shared culture medium through distinct, strain-specific nutrient conversions. B. longum 35624 deamidated nicotinamide to nicotinic acid and produced the tryptophan catabolite indole 3 lactic acid, whereas B. animalis subsp. lactis catabolised purine nucleosides and accumulated hypoxanthine; the two strains also differed in carbohydrate utilisation. EVs, purified by ultracentrifugation and size exclusion chromatography and characterised by nanoparticle tracking analysis, immunoassay and electron microscopy, carried a sparse small-molecule cargo. A membrane glycolipid represented the clearest vesicle-associated signal of bacterial origin, whereas bile acid and N acyl lipid conjugates were also detected but could not be attributed to bacterial production, as they were present in the culture medium. Together, these data provide a first reference description of the Bifidobacterium exometabolome and EV metabolome and identify strain specific extracellular metabolic activities as priorities for targeted validation.

papers.title: Temporal blood sampling improves parameter recovery in a model of enterohepatic bile acid circulation using surrogate-accelerated Bayesian inference
papers.abstract: Bile acids (BAs) are essential signaling molecules whose enterohepatic circulation (EHC) is disrupted across hepatobiliary disorders. Despite their potential as biomarkers, clinical utility is limited by high inter-individual variability, the inability of accessible peripheral blood to reflect true hepatic exposure, and the difficulty of directly measuring key physiological parameters governing the EHC. While mechanistic models can infer inaccessible hepatic profiles and patient-specific parameters from peripheral blood, personalizing them is computationally prohibitive due to multiscale dynamics causing numerical stiffness and the thousands of evaluations required for Bayesian inference. To overcome this, we developed an accelerated Bayesian inference pipeline combining timescale model reduction with neural network surrogates. Eigenvector participation factor analysis of a human EHC model revealed that rapid portal vein and hepatic sinusoidal transport drive stiffness. Applying the quasi-steady state approximation to these fast variables reduced integration times by over 97% with an integrated relative error 90% of the identifiability of five time points. Furthermore, the framework captured EHC compensatory dynamics, revealing a persistent positive correlation between intestinal transit and absorption. By making stiff EHC models tractable, our framework guides clinical study design and enables minimally invasive, mechanistic characterization of BA dysregulation, advancing our mechanistic understanding and personalized diagnosis of hepatobiliary diseases.

papers.title: A dominant SlTDM1 allele leads to unreduced gametes and polyploid offspring in tomato
papers.abstract: Engineering clonal reproduction through seeds typically requires the production of unreduced (2n) clonal gametes. Unreduced clonal gametes can be engineered through the Mitosis instead of Meiosis (MiMe) system, which so far has been developed in Arabidopsis, rice, tomato and Brassica napus. However, there is no universal genetic strategy to engineer MiMe as the factors regulating the number of meiotic cell divisions show functional divergence. A potential universal factor to abolish the second meiotic cell division is THREE DIVISIONS MUTANT1 (TDM1), which promotes the termination of meiosis in Arabidopsis and maize. Here, we developed transgenic tomato plants that express a tomato TDM1 allele (SlTDM1-P19L), which is expected to encode a phosphorylation-defective SlTDM1. We observed that SlTDM1-P19L lines produced a mixture of haploid and diploid gametes, which gave rise to up to 28% tetraploid selfing offspring from diploid parents with only mild effects on male fertility. In one line, the SlTDM1-P19L transgene led to co-suppression of the endogenous SlTDM1 gene, resulting in the production of hyper-reduced polyads rather than unreduced dyads or reduced tetrads, mimicking tdm1 null mutants. Together, our results show that the function of TDM1 is conserved in tomato, SlTDM1-P19L can be effective in producing unreduced gametes, and it is a promising factor to apply in MiMe system engineering.

papers.title: Pollen Ornamentation Morphospace: Interpretable Quantification by Persistent Homology
papers.abstract: Ornamentation, the sculpture of the outer pollen wall, is one of the central traits of pollen. However, it is mostly described with qualitative categories that rely on subjective judgment, and continuous, interpretable descriptors are still lacking. Here we used persistent homology, a fundamental method in topological data analysis, to define three interpretable descriptors (intensity, density and polarity) for three-dimensional pollen data. These descriptors form the three axes of a quantitative morphospace of pollen ornamentation, in which real, theoretical and ancestral pollen can be placed. The three axes were largely independent and separated common ornamentation types. In tests against known values, the morphospace recovered the number of ornamental elements in both theoretical pollen and real echinate pollen. Applied to pollination, it showed that, after phylogenetic correction, insect-pollinated pollen differed significantly from wind-pollinated pollen only in having more pronounced relief. In an evolutionary analysis within Asteraceae, it traced the three subfamilies diverging in different directions from their estimated common ancestor. By replacing qualitative categories with continuous, interpretable descriptors, this morphospace provides a common quantitative framework for pollen ornamentation. As three-dimensional pollen data accumulate, new grains can be placed in this morphospace without redefining the axes.

papers.title: Recurrent evolution of an APO1 cis-regulatory module that shapes rice panicle branching
papers.abstract: Quantitative variation in inflorescence branching drives grass diversification, yet the cis-regulatory mechanisms tuning reproductive meristem activity remain poorly understood. Here, we identified a module of two CArG boxes within a conserved noncoding sequence near rice APO1. Genome-edited alleles generated a quantitative phenotypic series: deletions affecting both CArG boxes produced the strongest increases in secondary branching, whereas deletions restricted to CArG box 1 produced smaller but reproducible increases. These deletions extended secondary branch formation toward the panicle base at the expense of direct spikelets, while spikelet number per primary branch was maintained or increased. Across eight genotypes, APO1 transcript abundance was quantitatively associated with branching, and both CArG boxes contributed to MADS15-MADS34 binding to CNS3, consistent with this module limiting APO1 expression. Structural and CArG-box changes in this region were detected across multiple phylogenetically distinct lineages with branched inflorescences, indicating that APO1 underwent recurrent cis-regulatory modification during grass inflorescence diversification.

papers.title: Low serine-glycine-one-carbon pathway activity defines purine salvage dependence in neuroblastoma
papers.abstract: MYCN amplification promotes serine-glycine-one-carbon (SGOC) metabolism in neuroblastoma, creating an intrinsic difference in SGOC activity between MYCNamplified and non-MYCN-amplified high-risk tumors. This metabolic distinction provides a model to investigate how SGOC activity shapes purine metabolism. Here, we show that non-MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines exhibit lower SGOC pathway activity and are more resistant to pharmacologic suppression of SGOC metabolism by SHMT inhibition under serine- and glycine-deprived conditions. Stable-isotope tracing revealed that non-MYCN-amplified cells exhibited lower contribution of serine-derived glycine and one-carbon units to de novo purine synthesis but elevated basal hypoxanthine and adenine salvage. These cells also showed greater preservation of adenylate pools during SHMT inhibition. Genetic depletion of APRT or HPRT1 preferentially impaired proliferation of non-MYCN-amplified cells, demonstrating increased salvage dependence. SHMT inhibition increased purine salvage, providing additional evidence that suppression of SGOC metabolism shifts purine production toward salvage. We also identify methionine salvage as an endogenous source of adenine that supports proliferation during SHMT inhibition through an MTAP-adenine-APRT axis. Together, these findings establish SGOC pathway activity as an intrinsic determinant of whether cells preferentially rely on de novo purine synthesis or purine salvage and identify salvage dependence as a potential therapeutic vulnerability of low-SGOC tumors.

papers.title: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produces synergistic anti-tumour activity across preclinical glioblastoma models
papers.abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains difficult to treat because of tumour heterogeneity and the limited activity of single-target therapies. Our previous phenotypic drug screen identified JAK2/STAT3 signalling and HSP90-dependent protein homeostasis as pharmacological vulnerabilities. We investigated whether combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition could produce broader anti-tumour activity across GBM models. Methods: Multiple JAK2 and HSP90 inhibitors were tested alone and in combination across 2- and 3-dimensional patient-derived GBM stem cell models. Drug interactions were quantified using the zero-interaction potency (ZIP) synergy model. Mechanistic studies included RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, western blotting, immunofluorescence and FUCCI live-cell imaging. Activity was also assessed in cerebral organoid GBM co-cultures, non-malignant human neural and glial cells and orthotopic GBM xenografts. Results: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produced synergistic interactions in 12 of the 13 GBM cell lines tested, using multiple structurally distinct inhibitor pairs. Gandotinib and NMS-E973 were selected for further mechanistic studies, where the combination reduced spheroid growth and increased caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage. Combination treatment was associated with G2/M accumulation, altered mitotic regulation, abnormal chromosome and spindle organisation, and increased gamma-H2AX signalling. Anti-tumour combination activity was maintained in cerebral organoid co-cultures, where tumour burden was reduced as assessed by imaging, histological and luciferase-based measurements, while the drug combination had relatively limited effects on non-malignant human neural and glial cell types tested over the same concentration range. In vivo, combined Pacritinib and NMS-E973 treatment significantly reduced tumour burden in orthotopic G7 xenografts compared with vehicle or either single agent. Conclusions: JAK2/HSP90 co-inhibition produces reproducible anti-tumour activity across heterogeneous GBM models and disrupts cell-cycle and mitotic progression. These findings support further evaluation of this combination strategy in GBM.

papers.title: Ecotypes matter: photoperiod and site of origin underlie the onset of leaf senescence in Eriophorum vaginatum, an Arctic foundation species
papers.abstract: The rapid warming of the Arctic is causing the growing season to expand and the climate to become more unpredictable. This scenario is intensifying a crucial trade-off arctic plants face: maximizing growth during the short growing season while avoiding freezes at the shoulder seasons. In response, ecotypes have evolved phenological behaviors that are finely tuned to their local climate, which often involves the use of photoperiod cues, especially in the fall. Under the rearrangement of temperature and light regimes, however, such phenological adaptations might prevent native plants from taking advantage of longer growing seasons. To test this phenological mechanism of local adaptation we used a decade-long reciprocal transplant experiment in Northern Alaska and observed the effects of seasonal light and temperature regimes on the leaf phenology of an arctic foundation species, Eriophorum vaginatum. We found that ecotypes rely heavily on site-specific photoperiod cues, but may also use temperature cues. These results indicate that local adaptation of this widespread species to local climates required the evolution of diverging phenological responses to seasonal changes in light. Because light cues will remain stable as the shoulder seasons expand, these adaptations are increasingly maladaptive, and could leave Eriophorum vulnerable to more competitive species.

papers.title: Evolution of sex-specific hormesis in a toxic niche specialist
papers.abstract: Ecological specialists often exploit toxic niches that can exclude competitors, predators and pathogens. Whether such specialization has intrinsic fitness benefits remains unclear. We address this question through study of Drosophila sechellia, a specialist on noni fruit, which is toxic for other insects. A noni diet did not affect innate behaviors but increased female reproductive fitness, lifespan and stress resistance, and biased offspring sex ratios towards females. These traits were linked to female-specific lipid accumulation upon noni consumption. Strikingly, noni's principal toxin, octanoic acid, reproduced these female-specific phenotypes, exhibiting a dose-dependent, biphasic - or hormetic - effect. The beneficial effects of octanoic acid require Alkbh7, a conserved mitochondrial protein involved in fatty acid metabolism. Finally, modelling showed fecundity and female bias can jointly maximize population growth. These results reveal how evolution of hormesis, to confer nutritious value upon a toxin, yields sexually-dimorphic fitness benefits, including an unusual uncoupling of reproductive fitness and lifespan.

papers.title: Limitations of gene-dense datasets for inferring relationships in rapid radiations: An example from the Ice Plants
papers.abstract: Premise: Aizoaceae (ice plants) are among the most rapidly radiating plant families on Earth, making them among the most difficult clades in the tree of life to resolve. Large, gene-rich datasets have been a powerful tool for exploring contentious relationships, and the Aizoaceae are an ideal model for testing the limits of gene-rich datasets for inferring the tree of life. Methods: In this study, we assembled a phylotranscriptomic dataset comprising 28 newly sequenced and 11 publicly available transcriptomes to infer relationships within the Aizoaceae. We inferred gene trees from 4,845 putative orthologs extracted from 15,818 homologous gene families, which we also used to infer gene duplications. We tested whether gene-tree filtering approaches could identify gene subsets that resolve relationships within the clade. Results: We found that, regardless of the gene-filtering approach or species-tree estimation, relationships among the Aizoaceae were largely congruent. Relationships within the subfamily Ruschioideae still showed little gene tree concordance. Our simulations show that inferring relationships within rapid radiations may be impossible because of short internodal branch lengths, regardless of the number of genes sampled. Gene duplication analysis at the base of the radiations provides candidates that potentially contributed to adaptations driving the radiation. Conclusions: This study highlights that rapid radiations can be difficult to infer because of pervasive incomplete lineage sorting and noise, and that limited information within individual genes may make methods that rely on gene trees unsuitable for these relationships. This appears to be the case in Aizoaceae; however, these limitations suggest that synteny-based analyses will play an important role in future investigations of the tree of life.
